Genre, audience, and purpose override that register: a letter, a speech and an advertisement keep their own character. The selected genre governs craft and form; the resolved language governs idiom, syntax and typography. Examples here illustrate meanings, not English phrases to translate.

## Reader and progression

Give the intended reader what they need to understand, judge or do the thing the text is for. Keep a clear focus, introduce unfamiliar concepts before the reasoning needs them, and order material by that reader's needs rather than the writer's discovery process. Relevant technical detail belongs; unexplained jargon and unrelated background do not.

Make the relations between passages real. A transition may explain a connection, but cannot invent one. Keep paragraphs coherent and give supporting material a clear place beside what it supports. The body and its sections remain intelligible without treating a title, standfirst or subheading as their opening sentence.

Open on something specific to the subject. End with what the job calls for: an earned understanding, conclusion, recommendation or next step. Remove introductions and conclusions that add only an announcement or a generic flourish.

## Expression

Use concrete words, useful verbs and a natural, varied cadence. Keep terminology and reference clear; introduce an unfamiliar abbreviation before using it alone. Choose ordinary words where they suffice and established specialist terms where they give this reader precision.

Let tone and rhetorical devices serve the genre and the meaning. A useful analogy, question, image, fragment or humorous turn can clarify or carry a voice; decoration and manufactured drama cannot. An imagined comparison is recognisable as a comparison, never presented as an event or someone's experience. Criticism addresses the supported issue without inventing motives or patronising the reader.

Each passage earns its place. Repetition may establish an independent entry point, explain a hard idea or give a deliberate rhetorical return; merely saying the same thing again does none of these. Keep formatting useful: headings for orientation, lists for coordinate items, tables for comparisons, emphasis for what merits it. Hold voice, terminology and presentation consistent unless a visible purpose calls for a change.

## Claims

Every claim is supported by the text or its material, with exact attribution and proportionate strength. Preserve the state of knowledge: what is unknown or unclaimed is not thereby known not to have happened. Keep uncertainty where it exists and certainty where it is warranted. A fact, quotation, source, scene, personal experience or opinion attributed to somebody is never invented to complete a form. Name the actual source of an attributed claim rather than invoking unnamed studies or experts.

Circumstantial detail is a claim too: duration, manner, motive, absence and background all need support. So does an evaluative characterisation: calling a count high, low or modest needs a comparison, target, capacity or speaker assessment. Otherwise give the count with its exclusions, without that assessment.

A sequence or correlation establishes no cause. A causal verb such as *shortened* needs causal support; a causal hedge such as *suggests that it shortened* still adds that attribution. This boundary holds in the title, summary, headings and body alike. Preserve chronology, scope and qualifications wherever a claim appears.

A stated length constrains the use of material and is never a licence to add to it. When the material is insufficient, deliver the length the material supports and name what further material would close the gap. A supplied publication limit is binding; meeting it cannot justify invention or loss of a qualification that changes a claim.
# Craft for five web genres

For article, casestudy, column and opinion, work as a skilled Swedish journalist at the professional level of SvD, DN, DI, Fokus, Ny Teknik, Filter or Forskning & Framsteg. For webcopy, work as an experienced Swedish copywriter and UX writer trusted by leading agencies and brands. These are standards of craft, not voices to imitate.

In every target language, keep that Swedish editorial or communicative tradition in the angle, disposition, storytelling, address and tone. ## Web reading

Give the reader a clear angle or task and useful ways into the text. Let facts and reasoning carry explanation; choose any narrative devices for what they contribute. Headline

Lead

- *Most* states what is typical across the whole text; each single paragraph or section follows its own content.

A text conforms when every part is present in the order shown and all three hold. Limits are exact; verify each one by counting.

A review of a finished text reports a part the text lacks as missing rather than writing it, and repairs only the parts the text has.

## Order

```text
Headline
Standfirst
Byline
Lead
Subheading        ┐ a section; one or more
Paragraphs        ┘
Last subheading   ┐ the ending
Paragraphs        ┘
```

Each part appears once, except the section, which repeats. The first subheading follows the lead directly. The body is everything from the lead through the ending.

The headline is the text's level-1 heading (HTML `h1`, Markdown `#`), and every subheading is a level-2 heading (HTML `h2`, Markdown `##`). The text should use these two levels only. Where an academic text would nest a level-3 heading, a further level-2 subheading usually serves; a level-3 heading is for the rare text whose structure truly demands one.

## Headline

- 20–70 characters, spaces included.
- It should be three to eight words and at most 60 characters.
- It is written as [Headlines](headlines.md) says.

## Standfirst

The standfirst is a summarising paragraph that introduces the article and stands on its own. It is a full paragraph; a deck — a subtitle or one-line teaser — is a different device and no substitute for it.

- One paragraph, at most 60 words.
- Self-contained: a reader who sees only the standfirst understands it fully.
- It says what the article is about and what the reader gains from reading it.
- It entices the reader to read on.

## Byline

One line naming the author. In English: `By <author>`. In another language, that language's conventional byline form. The author is the one the brief names; when it names none, the author is the user.

## Lead

The lead is the first paragraph of the body: one paragraph, meeting every requirement under *Paragraphs*. It introduces the subject and gives the reader a clear expectation of what they will learn by reading on.

### Standfirst and lead

Both open the text. Each works without the other, and read together they never repeat:

- The body reads complete without the standfirst, which is often shown apart from the body or skipped. The lead introduces every person, thing and event it mentions, and nothing in the body points back to the standfirst.
- They should begin with different first words, and an everyday word such as *the* or *it* counts like any other.
- Read in sequence, the lead advances. A reader who has just read the standfirst meets the lead as new material, never as the standfirst said again; what the body needs from the standfirst is named again in passing, and the lead moves on.

## Paragraphs

- Each paragraph holds one thought, and the thought sets its length. Most paragraphs come to two or three sentences. A thought that takes one sentence, or four or five, gets exactly that.
- A break may also fall for drama: a single sentence, or a single word, stands alone when isolating it creates an effect the text needs.
- Sentence length varies within the paragraph, giving the text a natural rhythm.
- A paragraph should be at most 80 words, so that a web reader takes it in at a glance. Eighty is the outer edge; aim well below it.

## Subheadings and sections

A section is a subheading plus the paragraphs under it.

- A subheading is at most 70 characters, spaces included.
- It describes clearly what the paragraphs under it are about, and it is written as [Headlines](headlines.md) says.
- A section holds at least one paragraph and should hold at most three. Most sections hold two or three.

## Ending

The ending is a section of its own, opened by its own subheading, after at least one other section. It is the last section, and it is short: one paragraph can be enough. It does two things:

- It shows that the expectation the lead set has been met.
- It calls the reader to action, and the action follows from the article's content. The selected genre says what that action is in its kind of text.

The last section is the ending when its subheading and paragraphs close the piece — the call to action, the reflection, the recommendation or the next step — and it opens no new line of argument. Stating the recommendation or proposal the text has built towards is closing content, even where the last section is the first place the text states it in full; so are the writer's own reservation about it and the call to try or adopt it. What makes a section carry the argument is reasons or evidence the conclusion rests on that no earlier section gave. A last section that states the proposal, admits a doubt about it and asks the reader to act on it brings none, and is the ending. A section that carries the argument with a closing line appended is not an ending.
# Headlines

How a headline is written, in any genre that links this file. A headline lets the reader judge at once whether the text is for them: it states the core of the text as briefly and precisely as it can, and it is understood on its own, with no image, standfirst or surrounding page to explain it. *Headline* here covers a text's subheadings too; for a subheading, the text is its section.

## Statement or label

A text that reports, explains, argues, decides or narrates gets a statement headline: a clause that says what the text says. A text the reader looks things up in or navigates by — a policy, a manual, opening hours, a contact page — gets a plain label naming what it holds: *Privacy policy*, where a statement would read *How we protect your data*. Everything below is about the statement headline.

## What a statement headline does

- It states the angle: the single most important message, the sentence that would remain if only one could. A subject alone is a label. Test: the headline could not head a different text on the same subject.
- It is a simple clause — subject, active verb, object where there is one — in straight word order, and in the present tense where that fits: *Council introduces free bus travel*.
- The most important keyword comes first.
- A concrete detail stands in it when the detail carries the message: a number, a date, a place. *Three schools to close this autumn* beats *Changes to school organisation*.
- The reader sees what they gain: a decision, a fact, a change. An instructional text may address the reader directly (*you*, *your*) and open on *How to*, *Why* or *Here's*.
- It is as short as the angle allows. Modifiers, repetition and filler go; a keyword that carries meaning stays. The format the text follows sets the limits.
- It sounds like something a person would say aloud.
- Its words are ones this audience knows. A technical term is the right keyword for specialists and noise for a general reader, and the same holds for names and abbreviations.
- Its tone is the text's tone, and never louder. Illness, accidents, crime and crises get a sober, understated headline; a light text can carry more personality.
- It is plain before it is clever. It works in full for a reader who misses every allusion, so a pun or a reference never carries the meaning.
- It gives the answer. Journalists hold a question headline to be the wrong form, and so does this: it is a deliberate exception, natural over a text built as questions and answers, and available where the text truly leaves the question open and the headline is meant to assert nothing.
- The verb does the work. A colon standing in for a verb, a clipped quotation and headline-speak all give way to the full clause.
- It complements what follows. Headline and standfirst, or subheading and the first sentence under it, say different things in different words.

## Every word supported

A headline claims only what its text claims. Every figure, name, claim and conclusion in it is in the text, at the text's own strength: never sharper, never more general, never a conclusion the text does not draw. A reader who finishes the text finds that the headline told the truth about it.

## A subheading over a quotation

A quotation in a section is there to carry what only its speaker can say: a judgement, a figure, a concession. A subheading standing over it, however far down the section the quotation stands, leaves that to the quotation. It states the section's angle from what the rest of the section says, or, where the quotation is the section's point, names the subject, the occasion or the speaker the quotation speaks to, and not the point itself. Test: a reader who has just read the subheading meets the quotation as new material, never as the subheading said again. *The clinic would double its training time*, over a head nurse saying *Next time I would double the training time before we switch*, has spent the quotation before the reader reaches it; *The head nurse looks back on the switch* leaves it to her.

The quotation bridge is the narrative sentence or clause that stands immediately before a quotation and leads the reader into it, including a speech tag that carries anything besides the attribution. The genre that quotes says what a quotation bridge may carry. A subheading standing over a quotation is outside the quotation bridge and is governed by this section.

## Getting there

Settle the reader and the angle before wording anything. Then write three to five variants and keep the clearest, which is rarely the cleverest. Word a subheading from its whole section, once the section is written, in words its first sentence does not use, and leave a quotation standing under it the judgement, figure or concession it is there to carry.
# Quoting speech

Read this before putting quotation marks around anything somebody said. It applies to interview transcripts, recorded remarks, meeting notes, and any other material where the words are a person's rather than a document's.

Speech is not written prose, and a transcript quoted raw reads as carelessness towards the speaker rather than fidelity to them. So a spoken quotation may be repaired — cautiously, within a boundary that is easier to state than to feel your way to.

When translating permitted quotations, preserve meaning, stance, certainty and distinctive voice in idiomatic target-language speech, not source-language syntax. The restrictions below protect that substance; they do not require word-for-word translation. Make an implicit referent explicit only when the supplied context settles it. Where the meaning remains ambiguous, paraphrase what is established rather than inventing a fluent interpretation.

## What may be repaired

The syntax of speech: a sentence abandoned halfway and restarted, a subject left behind by its verb, a clause that never closes. Fillers — *you know*, *sort of*, *liksom*, *alltså* — where they carry nothing. Repetition that is the speaker searching for a word rather than insisting on one. False starts, and the small disfluencies a person does not hear themselves make.

That is the whole list. Everything on it is noise the speaker did not intend to produce, and removing it leaves what they meant to say.

## What may not

**Meaning.** Not narrowed, not widened, not sharpened. A speaker who said *most of them* has not said *all of them*, and one who said *we looked at it* has not said *we rejected it*.

**Stance.** Approval stays approval, reluctance stays reluctance, and a speaker who was careful not to blame anybody is not made to blame somebody by a tidier sentence.

**Certainty.** *I think*, *probably*, *as far as I know*, and *we are not sure yet* are the claim, not padding on it. Removing a hedge manufactures a confidence the speaker did not have; adding one takes away a confidence they did.

**Distinctive wording.** Where the speaker reached for an unusual word, an image, a piece of slang, or a phrasing that is theirs, it stays. Smoothing it into the register of the surrounding article is the most tempting of these failures and the one a reader can least detect.

**A self-correction.** Where a speaker gives a number or a fact and then corrects it, the correction is what they said. Quoting the first version is a misquotation; quoting a version that never existed — the correction with the correcting away — is worse.

**Anything additive.** Add no new meaning: no fact, stance, certainty, name, figure or connection that the speaker did not supply. A permitted repair or translation may change words only to render that same meaning.

## When to paraphrase instead

Where fidelity is uncertain, paraphrase. A paraphrase that attributes carefully — *she said the change had taken about a year, and that she was not sure it would hold* — is accurate, useful, and honest about what the material supports. A fluent direct quotation assembled out of a fragmentary answer is none of those things, however good it sounds.

The cases that should turn into paraphrase: material that is a summary of what somebody said rather than their words; a transcript too broken to repair inside the boundary above; several remarks that would have to be welded together to make one sentence; and any moment where you find yourself choosing between two readings of what the speaker meant.

Signal what the material actually is. Where the source is notes rather than a recording, the text says what the person said and does not pretend to their exact wording.

## What stays outside this

Whether the speaker approves the quotation. Quote approval is a human arrangement between the writer and the person quoted, and nothing here verifies it or stands in for it. A draft may say a quotation is unapproved; it may not treat the absence of approval as a problem it has solved.

draft = '''# School temperature readings leave causes unresolved

For municipal property managers, Björkskolan’s four-week trial offers a practical lesson in reading measurements: check what was counted, where sensors stood, and what the trial left unmeasured before using the results to guide heating decisions.

By the user

In January 2026, the fictional municipality of Lervik’s property office installed temperature sensors in six classrooms at Björkskolan. It wanted to find out whether complaints about cold air coincided with low temperatures during lessons. Understanding the results starts with the distinction between a recorded temperature and what that reading can establish.

## A lesson count leaves duration unknown

The report *Mätförsök i Björkskolan*, dated March 12, 2026, records 14 of 120 lesson periods with at least one reading below 20°C. Sensors recorded values every five minutes over four weeks. The report does not say how long temperatures stayed below that threshold or whether students felt cold.

The 20°C threshold was the office’s own working limit for the trial, rather than a statement of a legal requirement. A whole-day average can conceal temperature changes during lessons, so the report presents lesson periods instead of a single daily average. Read the 14-period count as a count of periods containing a reading below the threshold, rather than a measure of time spent below it.

## Sensor location defines the reading

A temperature sensor measures the temperature where it sits. Two sensors stood near exterior walls and four on interior walls. Their locations were documented, but the trial did not experimentally compare those placements.

Air temperature is also different from operative temperature, a measure that accounts for both air temperature and heat radiation from surrounding surfaces. The trial measured only air temperature. Ventilation, drafts, and perceived temperature were not measured, and the results cover only these six rooms and these four weeks.

## Rask checks operating schedules

After the trial, operations technician Elin Rask reviewed the ventilation and heating schedules with the school’s caretaker. The effects of any adjustments have not yet been measured.

“We know when we need to take a closer look. We don’t yet know why it got cold at those particular times,” Rask said. She recommends linking temperature records to room-use times before changing the controls. A further trial is planned for November, with sensors placed the same way and notes on when rooms are used; funding has not been decided.

## Match the records to room use first

Before changing heating controls, follow Rask’s recommendation: connect the temperature readings to the times rooms are used. Keep the trial’s limits alongside its lesson count. It identifies periods to examine more closely; it does not establish the cause of the cold or show whether adjustments have worked.
'''
(scratch / 'draft.md').write_text(draft)

# Source and translated-quotation comparison

Complete source and complete draft were read. Scope: source support and translated speech only. The Claims section of the supplied editorial contract and the supplied quotations guidance were also read. No source or draft was changed, no browsing was performed, and no general editorial or mechanical review was undertaken.

## Findings

### S1 — Added administrative status

Draft: “the fictional municipality of Lervik’s property office”.

Source: “Fiktiva Lerviks fastighetskontor satte i januari 2026 temperaturgivare i sex klassrum i Björkskolan.” The brief identifies the audience as “kommunala fastighetsförvaltare”; that audience does not identify Lervik's administrative status.

Difference: the draft identifies Lervik as a municipality. The source names Lervik and its property office without supplying that classification. This is a source-support finding, not a preference between synonymous names.

Counterexample, source to draft: Lervik could be a locality whose named property office belongs to another municipal administration. All supplied facts, including the municipal-manager audience, remain true, while “municipality of Lervik” is false. No supplied statement excludes this case. In the other direction, “municipality of Lervik” would imply the named office and municipality but would not contradict the source's less specific place reference; the unsupported addition lies in the draft's narrower classification.

Smallest supported repair: “the fictional Lervik’s property office” or, more naturally, “Lervik’s fictional property office”. Either retains the supplied fictional status and office without inventing a municipal classification.

### S2 — Added recording agent

Draft: “Sensors recorded values every five minutes over four weeks.”

Source: “Värden registrerades var femte minut under fyra veckor.” The preceding sentence establishes installation of temperature sensors, but does not identify what registered their output.

Difference: the interval and duration are preserved, but a passive statement about recorded values becomes a statement that the sensors performed the recording.

Counterexample, source to draft: sensors could provide temperature outputs to a separate logger that records them every five minutes for four weeks. The source would hold, while the literal claim that the sensors recorded the values would not. Nothing in the supplied material rules out a separate logger. In the other direction, sensors recording values at the stated interval and duration would necessarily produce recorded values as described by the source; the draft adds an agent rather than omitting the measurement event.

Smallest supported repair: “Values were recorded every five minutes over four weeks.”

### T1 — Temporal plurality supplied inside translated speech

Draft: “We don’t yet know why it got cold at those particular times”.

Source: “Vi vet ännu inte varför det blev kallt just då.” Full quote: “Vi vet när vi behöver titta närmare. Vi vet ännu inte varför det blev kallt just då.”

Difference: “just då” points emphatically to the relevant time, without specifying a set of multiple times. “those particular times” makes that implicit temporal reference explicitly plural. Neither the count of 14 lesson periods nor the speaker's “när” settles that this particular remark refers to multiple cold events. This is a translated-quotation finding, including an unsupported number assertion within the translation.

Counterexample, source to draft: Rask could be referring to one particular episode selected for closer examination, although the report counted 14 lesson periods with at least one reading under the office's working threshold. The supplied quote and the rest of the material would remain true, but a quotation attributing multiple particular cold times to Rask would not. No supplied statement excludes this case. In the other direction, Rask could have multiple occasions in mind; Swedish “just då” can accommodate a contextual temporal reference, so that case does not make the source false. The defect is resolving a reference that the supplied context leaves open.

Smallest supported repair: “We don’t yet know why it got cold right then.” This is idiomatic American speech and retains the emphatic temporal reference without supplying plurality.

## Complete claim accounting

Each entry quotes the source wording that supports the draft's claim, including qualifications that apply across its clauses. Repeated propositions in headings, lead, and ending are accounted for separately.

1. **Title: “School temperature readings leave causes unresolved.”** Source: “Vi vet ännu inte varför det blev kallt just då”; also “Ingen … orsak till kyla … följer av materialet.” The school setting is supplied by “sex klassrum i Björkskolan.” The title identifies the limits of the readings; it neither assigns a cause nor denies that a cause exists. “Unresolved” preserves the material's present knowledge limit. No finding.

2. **Lead: “For municipal property managers”.** Source brief: “Skriv en pedagogisk webbartikel för kommunala fastighetsförvaltare som kan värmesystem men inte mätteknik.” Subject and audience agree. The draft does not assert that the reader lacks knowledge of heating systems. No finding.

3. **Lead: “Björkskolan’s four-week trial”.** Source: “Fiktiva Lerviks fastighetskontor satte i januari 2026 temperaturgivare i sex klassrum i Björkskolan”; “Värden registrerades var femte minut under fyra veckor.” The possessive marks the school's trial location, not ownership of the office or sensors. Duration and school agree. No finding.

4. **Lead: “offers a practical lesson in reading measurements: check what was counted, where sensors stood, and what the trial left unmeasured before using the results to guide heating decisions.”** Source: “14 av totalt 120 registrerade lektionspass innehöll minst en mätning under 20 grader Celsius”; “Två givare stod nära ytterväggar, fyra på innerväggar”; “Ventilation, luftdrag och upplevd temperatur mättes inte”; “Hon rekommenderar att koppla temperaturserier till användningstider innan man ändrar styrningen.” This is the article's own supported instruction, not an attributed expert opinion or a claim that heating changes occurred. Its premises are the count, locations, omitted measurements, and recommendation. No finding.

5. **Byline: “By the user”.** No personal author name is supplied: “Ingen byline är given.” Under the resolved instructions, this identifies the invoking user, not a person inferred from the reporting material. It supplies no invented named source or personal experience. No finding.

6. **Opening: “In January 2026 … property office installed temperature sensors in six classrooms at Björkskolan.”** Source: “Fiktiva Lerviks fastighetskontor satte i januari 2026 temperaturgivare i sex klassrum i Björkskolan.” Time, office, installation, device type, number, room type, and location agree. The classification “municipality” is unsupported as detailed in S1. Fictional status is explicitly supplied both here and by the synthetic-material notice.

7. **Opening: “It wanted to find out whether complaints about cold air coincided with low temperatures during lessons.”** Source: “Kontoret ville veta om klagomål på kall luft sammanföll med låga temperaturer under lektionstid.” Actor, motive, question, temporal scope, and uncertainty agree. The draft does not say the intended association was found. No finding.

8. **Opening: “Understanding the results starts with the distinction between a recorded temperature and what that reading can establish.”** Source brief: “Vinkel: vad ett kort mätförsök kan och inte kan säga om värmen i en skola”; material: “En givare mäter temperaturen där den sitter”; “Den säger heller inte om eleverna frös.” This is the author's organizing argument from supported distinctions. It invents no empirical effect or attributed opinion. No finding.

9. **Heading: “A lesson count leaves duration unknown.”** Source: “Rapporten … anger att 14 av totalt 120 registrerade lektionspass innehöll minst en mätning under 20 grader Celsius. Den säger inte hur länge temperaturen låg under gränsen.” In context, “unknown” describes what this report's count establishes, not what every person could know from other information. It preserves the knowledge boundary without claiming the duration was zero. No finding.

10. **Report identity and date: “The report Mätförsök i Björkskolan, dated March 12, 2026”.** Source: “Rapporten Mätförsök i Björkskolan, daterad 12 mars 2026”. Name, document type, calendar date, and attribution agree. No finding.

11. **Count: “records 14 of 120 lesson periods with at least one reading below 20°C.”** Source: “anger att 14 av totalt 120 registrerade lektionspass innehöll minst en mätning under 20 grader Celsius.” The count concerns lesson periods, not individual low readings, and retains “at least one” and the strict below-threshold relation. The total denominator is retained. No high/low assessment is added. No finding.

12. **Recording: “Sensors recorded values every five minutes over four weeks.”** Source: “Värden registrerades var femte minut under fyra veckor.” What was measured, interval, and duration agree; recording agency differs as detailed in S2.

13. **Knowledge limits: “The report does not say how long temperatures stayed below that threshold or whether students felt cold.”** Source: “Den säger inte hur länge temperaturen låg under gränsen. Den säger heller inte om eleverna frös.” Both statements concern what the report says, not the actual absence of low temperatures or cold feelings. “Students felt cold” conveys “eleverna frös” in this temperature context without adding health outcomes. Duration is unquantified in both. No finding.

14. **Threshold: “The 20°C threshold was the office’s own working limit for the trial, rather than a statement of a legal requirement.”** Source: “Gränsen 20 grader var kontorets egen arbetsgräns för försöket, inte ett påstående om ett rättsligt krav.” Ownership of the chosen limit, trial scope, numerical threshold, and distinction from a legal claim all agree. This does not assert that no legal requirement exists. No finding.

15. **Daily average and report presentation: “A whole-day average can conceal temperature changes during lessons, so the report presents lesson periods instead of a single daily average.”** Source: “Ett medelvärde för hela dagen kan dölja variation under lektionerna. Rapporten redovisar därför lektionspass i stället för ett enda dygnsmedelvärde.” Conditional possibility “can” is retained. The explanatory “so” corresponds to the source's explicit “därför”; this connection is supplied, not inferred from sequence. Whole-day and daily averages denote the same averaging period in this context. No finding.

16. **Interpretive instruction: “Read the 14-period count as a count of periods containing a reading below the threshold, rather than a measure of time spent below it.”** Source: “14 av totalt 120 registrerade lektionspass innehöll minst en mätning under 20 grader Celsius. Den säger inte hur länge temperaturen låg under gränsen.” This supported inference preserves the unit counted and distinguishes it from duration. “A reading” in this instruction is existential and does not reduce “at least one” to exactly one. No finding.

17. **Heading: “Air readings omit part of the thermal picture.”** Source: “Operativ temperatur är ett annat mått som tar hänsyn till både luftens temperatur och värmestrålningen från omgivande ytor; försöket mätte bara lufttemperatur”; “Ventilation, luftdrag och upplevd temperatur mättes inte.” The heading is a qualitative summary of those explicit measurement omissions, not a claim that the unmeasured factors caused cold. No finding.

18. **Sensor scope: “A temperature sensor measures the temperature where it sits.”** Source: “En givare mäter temperaturen där den sitter.” Generic device and local scope agree. No finding.

19. **Sensor placement: “Two sensors stood near exterior walls and four on interior walls.”** Source: “Två givare stod nära ytterväggar, fyra på innerväggar.” Device counts and the asymmetry between near and on are retained. In this building context, exterior/outer walls and interior/inner walls identify the same respective wall categories. No finding.

20. **Placement evidence: “Their locations were documented, but the trial did not experimentally compare those placements.”** Source: “Givarnas placering dokumenterades men jämfördes inte experimentellt.” Documentation is asserted, experimental comparison denied. The draft does not generalize that no nonexperimental comparison occurred. No finding.

21. **Operative temperature: “Air temperature is also different from operative temperature, a measure that accounts for both air temperature and heat radiation from surrounding surfaces.”** Source: “Operativ temperatur är ett annat mått som tar hänsyn till både luftens temperatur och värmestrålningen från omgivande ytor.” “Operative temperature” is the corresponding technical term in the context supplied, and both components and surrounding-surface scope are preserved. The draft does not claim that the two measured numbers always differ. No finding.

22. **Trial measure: “The trial measured only air temperature.”** Source: “försöket mätte bara lufttemperatur.” The exclusivity applies to the kind of temperature measured and is exactly supplied. No finding.

23. **Unmeasured factors and bounded coverage: “Ventilation, drafts, and perceived temperature were not measured, and the results cover only these six rooms and these four weeks.”** Source: “Ventilation, luftdrag och upplevd temperatur mättes inte”; “Mätningarna omfattar bara dessa sex rum och dessa fyra veckor.” Ventilation, air drafts, and perceived temperature correspond in this measurement context; none is replaced by a cause or quantified effect. Room and time limitations retain “only”. No finding.

24. **Heading: “November plans await a funding decision.”** Source: “Nästa försök planeras för november …; finansiering är inte beslutad.” In the immediately following text, this reads as the planned November trial's still-undecided funding status, not a claim that funding was refused or that the trial is certain to occur. “Await” adds no identified cause of delay or cancellation in this context. No finding.

25. **Post-trial activity: “After the trial, operations technician Elin Rask reviewed the ventilation and heating schedules with the school’s caretaker.”** Source: “Driftteknikern Elin Rask gick efter försöket igenom tiderna för ventilation och värme med skolans vaktmästare.” Named person, occupational role, completed review, chronological relation, subject of review, and other participant agree. “Schedules” identifies the operating times being reviewed, without adding rescheduling. “Caretaker” identifies the school's building-maintenance role denoted by “vaktmästare”, without assigning an additional job or action. No finding.

26. **Adjustment effects: “The effects of any adjustments have not yet been measured.”** Source: “Inga justeringars effekt har ännu mätts.” The absence concerns measurements of effects, not the existence of adjustments or effects. “Any” preserves the source's noncommitment about whether adjustments were made. No finding.

27. **Quote attribution and first sentence: “We know when we need to take a closer look,” Rask said.** Source: “Rask sade: ‘Vi vet när vi behöver titta närmare.’” The original is explicitly an exact interview utterance authorized for idiomatic translation: “Detta är ett ordagrant intervjuuttalande och får översättas idiomatiskt med bevarad innebörd.” Attribution, plural speaker perspective, certainty about knowing when, and need for closer examination agree. “Take a closer look” is ordinary American speech conveying “titta närmare”, preserving the plain direct voice. No finding.

28. **Quote second sentence: “We don’t yet know why it got cold at those particular times.”** Source: “Vi vet ännu inte varför det blev kallt just då.” First-person plural, present knowledge limit, “yet”, cause question, and past becoming cold agree. “It” is impersonal, as Swedish “det” is here. “Got cold” idiomatically conveys the change “blev kallt”. The explicit plural temporal reference differs as detailed in T1. The rest retains the contrast between known when and unknown why without adding a cause, stance, or hedge.

29. **Recommendation: “She recommends linking temperature records to room-use times before changing the controls.”** Source: “Hon rekommenderar att koppla temperaturserier till användningstider innan man ändrar styrningen.” Rask is the recommender. In this context the records are the time-indexed readings already described, so “temperature records” still denotes the measured series rather than an unrelated temperature document. Room-use times explicate the source's settled classroom-use reference, confirmed by “noteringar om när rummen används”. “Before” preserves the sequence in the recommendation, without asserting that control changes have occurred or are guaranteed to help. No finding.

30. **Next trial: “A further trial is planned for November, with sensors placed the same way and notes on when rooms are used; funding has not been decided.”** Source: “Nästa försök planeras för november med likadant placerade givare och noteringar om när rummen används; finansiering är inte beslutad.” Planned rather than promised status, month, equivalent placement, usage notes, and financing uncertainty agree. The draft supplies no date within November, guaranteed occurrence, or financing outcome. No finding.

31. **Closing heading: “Use the trial to guide further investigation.”** Source: “Vi vet när vi behöver titta närmare. Vi vet ännu inte varför det blev kallt just då”; “Hon rekommenderar att koppla temperaturserier till användningstider innan man ändrar styrningen.” This is the author's supported advocacy for follow-up, not an additional event or attributed opinion. No finding.

32. **Closing instruction: “Before changing heating controls, follow Rask’s recommendation: connect the temperature readings to the times rooms are used.”** Source: “Hon rekommenderar att koppla temperaturserier till användningstider innan man ändrar styrningen”; “tiderna för ventilation och värme”; “noteringar om när rummen används.” This narrower application of the recommendation to heating controls fits the brief's school-heating angle. It does not attribute a new recommendation excluding ventilation controls to Rask. Temporal relationship and measured-series/usage linkage agree. No finding.

33. **Closing instruction: “Keep the trial’s limits alongside its lesson count.”** Source: “14 av totalt 120 registrerade lektionspass innehöll minst en mätning under 20 grader Celsius”; “Mätningarna omfattar bara dessa sex rum och dessa fyra veckor”; “Den säger inte hur länge temperaturen låg under gränsen. Den säger heller inte om eleverna frös.” This is supported advice about reading the reported count with its qualifications. No invented fact or experience is presupposed. No finding.

34. **Closing capability and limits: “It identifies periods to examine more closely; it does not establish the cause of the cold or show whether adjustments have worked.”** Source: “Vi vet när vi behöver titta närmare. Vi vet ännu inte varför det blev kallt just då”; “Inga justeringars effekt har ännu mätts”; “Ingen … orsak till kyla … följer av materialet.” In context “it” denotes the trial and its results. The identification is for examination, not a diagnosis. Unknown cause and unmeasured adjustment effects stay unknown; neither absence of a cause nor failure of adjustments is asserted. No finding.

## Pronouns: person, number, and natural gender

- **“It” in the opening (“It wanted”)** refers to the property office. English third-person singular, nonpersonal organizational reference, corresponds to source “Kontoret”, a singular noun. Swedish neuter grammatical gender does not establish biological/natural gender; the draft makes none.
- **“it” in “where it sits”** is a singular sensor, corresponding to “En givare … där den sitter”. Swedish common grammatical gender “den” supplies no natural gender. English nonpersonal “it” adds none.
- **“Their locations”** refers to the six sensors already counted. English third-person plural possessive corresponds to plural “Givarnas placering”. Plurality is supported by “Två givare … fyra”. No human or natural-gender assertion is made.
- **“We” in both quote sentences** corresponds to “Vi” in each source sentence: first-person plural. Both include the speaker, but neither identifies the group's membership beyond that. The draft does not add group members or genders.
- **“it” in “it got cold”** corresponds to impersonal “det” in “det blev kallt”. Neither asserts a particular person's gender or an entity's singular count.
- **“those” in “those particular times”** explicitly supplies plural temporal referents where “just då” has no such number assertion. This is T1.
- **“She”** refers to Rask and matches the source's explicit “Hon rekommenderar”. The source establishes third-person singular feminine reference rather than the translation inferring natural gender from the name Elin. No added gender finding.
- **“its” in “its lesson count” and “It” in the last sentence** refer to the singular trial as expressed by “försöket”. No natural gender is asserted; Swedish neuter grammatical gender is not recast as such.
- Other demonstratives and possessives (“these six rooms”, “these four weeks”, “that threshold”, “office’s own”, and “school’s”) preserve the supplied counts, local scope, institutional reference, and threshold ownership. None supplies an unsupported person's gender or number.

## Translation assessment beyond T1

The permitted direct quotation retains its two short, plain declarations, the contrast between knowing when and not yet knowing why, plural first-person perspective, warranted certainty in the first sentence, and explicit uncertainty in the second. “Take a closer look” and “got cold” are idiomatic target-language speech. No distinctive unusual wording, self-correction, or meaningful disfluency appears in the supplied quote, and none has been deleted. The only concrete obstruction to fidelity is the explicit plural temporal reference in T1. Source-support differences outside quotation are reported under S1 and S2; no other term change yields a concrete contextual counterexample.

Completion status: COMPLETE. Complete draft claims and translated quotation compared against complete supplied material. Unresolved findings: S1 (added municipal classification), S2 (added recording agent), and T1 (plural temporal reference in translated speech). Report only; no draft repairs made.

- “where it sits” refers to the singular temperature sensor: “En givare … där den sitter.” Swedish “den” is grammatical common gender here, not a human natural-gender statement; English “it” does not invent one.

- “these six rooms” and “these four weeks” preserve the source demonstratives and exact restrictive quantities: “bara dessa sex rum och dessa fyra veckor.”

- A day whose average conceals within-lesson variation is compatible with both versions, as is a day whose average does not conceal such variation: both say “can”/“kan.” No actual variation or universal concealment is asserted.
- “Schedules” could name plans in another context, whereas Swedish “tiderna” could name times. Here the phrase specifies the ventilation and heating operating times that the technician reviewed. Here its referent is the supplied values taken every five minutes across four weeks, already described in the draft. A lone isolated reading would not be the referent of either recommendation here: “Värden registrerades var femte minut under fyra veckor” supplies the series. Linking those recorded series to use times satisfies both versions. No unrelated record type is introduced.
- An operative-temperature value equal to air temperature in some circumstances is compatible with both versions. The draft distinguishes the measures, and the source’s “ett annat mått” likewise distinguishes measures rather than requiring unequal numerical values.
- Funding eventually approved, declined, or still undecided is compatible with the current planning status in both versions. Neither predicts that the November trial will happen.

The draft’s “any adjustments” and final “show whether adjustments have worked” preserve that uncertainty rather than asserting an event or result.

## Translated quotation comparison

Source: “Vi vet när vi behöver titta närmare. Vi vet ännu inte varför det blev kallt just då.”

Draft: “We know when we need to take a closer look. We don’t yet know why it got cold right then,” Rask said.

The quotation is explicitly authorized for idiomatic translation. “Take a closer look” renders “titta närmare” as natural American speech while keeping the examination metaphor. “Need” preserves “behöver.” The direct, parallel “We know … We don’t yet know …” preserves the repeated first-person plural, the speaker’s stance, and the contrast between established timing and unresolved cause. The contraction is idiomatic spoken English and changes neither certainty nor distinctive voice. “Got cold” preserves the change expressed by “blev kallt”; “right then” preserves the time emphasis of “just då.” The translation does not add a measured duration, an identified cause, or an explicit member of “we.” No concrete obstruction to the same meaning and voice was found.

## Findings

Source-support findings: none. Translation findings: none. No repair proposed because the draft is defensible as written within this comparison’s scope. General editorial and mechanical review was not performed.
